items.stem: Explain how the position of items on a menu can influence food choice.
items.answer: Items at the beginning or end of a list (primacy and recency) or highlighted in boxes are noticed and remembered more, so they are chosen more often.

items.stem: Explain why restaurants may use descriptive labels on menus.
items.answer: Descriptions such as “locally grown” or “slow-cooked” create expectations of quality and taste, so diners are more likely to choose the dish and rate it more highly.

items.stem: Leila is redesigning the menu of a restaurant in Lagos to increase sales of the most profitable dishes. Explain why one of your suggestions might work.
items.answer: For example, descriptive labels create expectations of quality, so diners are more likely to choose those dishes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark feature; 1 mark psychological explanation [2]

items.stem: Mateo is redesigning the menu of a restaurant in Dubai to increase sales of the most profitable dishes. (a) Suggest two features of menu design Mateo could use. (b) Explain why one of your suggestions might work.
items.answer: (a) Place profitable dishes first in their section or in a highlighted box; add descriptive labels; remove currency symbols; use an expensive anchor dish. (b) For example, descriptive labels create expectations of quality, so diners are more likely to choose those dishes.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each [2] (b) 1 mark feature; 1 mark psychological explanation [2]

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of eye-tracking research on menu design. Include at least one point about usefulness.
items.answer: Strength (usefulness): Restaurants can design menus based on how people actually read them. Strength (objectivity): Eye tracking records exactly where and for how long people look, without relying on self-report. Weakness (ecological validity): Participants usually read menus in a laboratory with eye-tracking equipment, not while dining with friends. Weakness (validity): Looking at an item does not necessarily mean choosing it. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: A restaurant in Accra tested two menu designs. On 7 evenings the menu showed prices with a currency symbol and on 7 evenings prices were shown as plain numbers. Average spending per diner was recorded. Table: Average spend per diner ($) — Plain numbers: 34, 38, 35, 36, 33, 38, 34. With currency symbol: 28, 30, 31, 23, 32, 31, 34. (a) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (b) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: (a) The plain numbers condition had a higher mean (35.4) than the with currency symbol condition (29.9), suggesting that showing prices without a currency symbol increases spending. (b) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.

items.stem: Evaluate the PAD model of store atmosphere, including a discussion of measurement.

(b) There will be a difference in average spending per diner between diners given menus with plain-number prices and diners given menus with a currency symbol. (c) The plain numbers condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (d) Mean for plain numbers = 36.2 and with currency symbol = 33.0; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 11 and 9) and the sample is small (n = 9 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (e) Randomly allocate participants to the conditions, to reduce the effect of participant variables.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: IV; 1 mark: DV, operationalised [2] (b) 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2] (c) 1 mark: identifies the condition with the larger spread; 1 mark: explains that a larger SD means scores are more spread around the mean [2] (d) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (e) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3]

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “The tendency to remember and choose items presented first”?
items.answer: Primacy effect
items.markingKey: Primacy effect: the tendency to remember and choose items presented first. [1]

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain how the position of items on a menu can influence food choice. (b) In a revision session, a student says: “Menu design can influence how much diners spend.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: (a) Items at the beginning or end of a list (primacy and recency) or highlighted in boxes are noticed and remembered more, so they are chosen more often. (b) Correct. Price format, layout and descriptions all affect choices.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark position effect; 1 mark explanation [2] (b) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Eye-tracking research on menu design can be evaluated in terms of ecological validity. Explain one weakness of the study relating to this issue.
items.answer: Participants usually read menus in a laboratory with eye-tracking equipment, not while dining with friends.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to ecological validity; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Isla is redesigning the menu of a restaurant in Jakarta to increase sales of the most profitable dishes. Suggest two features of menu design Isla could use.
items.answer: Place profitable dishes first in their section or in a highlighted box; add descriptive labels; remove currency symbols; use an expensive anchor dish.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A restaurant in Bogotá tested two menu designs. On 7 evenings the menu showed prices with a currency symbol and on 7 evenings prices were shown as plain numbers. Average spending per diner was recorded. Table: Average spend per diner ($) — Plain numbers: 33, 40, 37, 31, 32, 33, 36. With currency symbol: 30, 28, 26, 34, 28, 30, 29. Write a directional (one-tailed) hypothesis for this study.
items.answer: Diners given menus with plain-number prices will spend more than diners given menus with a currency symbol.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: IV and DV both included (operationalised); 1 mark: correct form of hypothesis [2]

items.stem: Zara compared average spend per diner (in dollars) on evenings when menu prices included “$” and evenings when they were plain numbers. Table: Average spend per diner ($) — Plain numbers: 33, 31, 29, 31, 35, 35, 60. With currency symbol: 32, 23, 28, 29, 30, 31, 29. (a) Calculate the percentage of participants in the with currency symbol condition who scored 31 or more. Show your working. (b) Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: (a) 28.6% (b) Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 out of 7 participants scored 31 or more: 2 ÷ 7 × 100 = 28.6%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Design a field experiment to investigate whether diners choose healthier dishes when they are placed at the top of the menu. Your plan must include: the experimental design, ethical issues and the sampling technique.
items.answer: Method: a field experiment. Manipulate the IV in a natural everyday setting; participants may not know they are being studied; standardise as much of the procedure as possible. Variables: IV: position of healthy dishes; DV: number of healthy dishes ordered. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Santiago, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: A researcher in Mexico City is interested in where diners prefer to sit in a restaurant. Design an observation to test this. Your plan must include: the sampling technique, the type of observation, ethical issues and behavioural categories. Then explain one weakness of your plan and how it could be overcome.
items.answer: Method: an observation. Structured observation with operationalised behavioural categories and time sampling; two observers to check inter-rater reliability; overt or covert as appropriate. Variables: behaviour: seat choice; categories: wall seat, window seat, centre table, booth. Sample: for example an opportunity or volunteer sample of about 30 people from the target population in Mexico City, with reasons. Design/procedure: clear, replicable steps, with standardised instructions and random allocation or counterbalancing where relevant. Ethics: informed consent, right to withdraw, protection from harm, confidentiality and a full debrief. Data: quantitative scores summarised with means and a suitable graph; qualitative answers analysed into themes where collected. Weakness: for example a small or biased sample; overcome by a larger, more representative sample.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: a detailed, accurate and replicable plan using the stated method; all required features are included and are appropriate to the aim; variables are operationalised; ethics are addressed. Middle band: a workable plan with most required features but some lack detail or are not justified. Lower band: a basic plan with few features or with errors in method.

items.stem: Which term is defined as the following: “The distance between neighbouring tables in a restaurant”?
items.answer: Table spacing
items.markingKey: Table spacing: the distance between neighbouring tables in a restaurant. [1]

items.stem: Outline one weakness of research on table spacing in restaurants that relates to cultural differences.
items.answer: Preferred personal space differs between cultures, so findings from one country may not apply elsewhere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to cultural differences; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Explain one weakness of research on table spacing in restaurants in terms of self-report.
items.answer: Many studies ask diners to imagine or rate scenarios, which may not match their real behaviour.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies a relevant weakness linked to self-report; 1 mark: explained using detail from the study [2]

items.stem: Ines compared average spend per diner (in dollars) on evenings when menu prices included “$” and evenings when they were plain numbers. Table: Average spend per diner ($) — Plain numbers: 32, 35, 37, 39, 40, 39, 40, 37. With currency symbol: 33, 34, 26, 26, 32, 34, 35, 27. Calculate the range of scores for each condition.
items.answer: Plain numbers: 8; with currency symbol: 9.
items.markingKey: Plain numbers: 40 − 32 = 8; with currency symbol: 35 − 26 = 9. 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: A new restaurant in Istanbul has one large room with tables close together in rows. The manager, Tariq, notices that wall tables fill first and that couples ask to move. (a) Use prospect–refuge theory to explain why wall tables fill first. (b) Suggest one change to the seating and explain its benefit.
items.answer: (a) Wall tables provide refuge (protection from behind) and a view of the room (prospect), which people find comfortable. (b) Add booths or screens, or increase spacing, to give diners privacy and comfort, increasing satisfaction.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark prospect; 1 mark refuge [2] (b) 1 mark change; 1 mark benefit [2]

items.stem: What is meant by ‘approach behaviour’?
items.answer: Responses such as staying longer, exploring and spending more in an environment.
items.markingKey: Approach behaviour: responses such as staying longer, exploring and spending more in an environment. 1 mark for a partial definition; 2 marks for a full, accurate definition [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) A student writes: “A good mood always makes shoppers spend more.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how a store’s atmosphere can influence consumer behaviour, using the PAD model.
items.answer: (a) Not correct. Mood effects depend on the shopper, the product and the situation, and may be small. (b) Features such as music, lighting and scent affect shoppers’ pleasure and arousal (and feeling of control); pleasant, moderately arousing environments produce approach behaviours (staying, spending) while unpleasant ones produce avoidance.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: correct judgement; 1 mark: accurate explanation [2] (b) 1 mark atmosphere affects emotion; 1 mark approach/avoidance [2]

items.stem: Explain one strength of the PAD model of store atmosphere relating to supporting evidence and one weakness relating to reductionism.
items.answer: Strength (supporting evidence): Studies of music, scent and lighting show effects on time spent and evaluations, as the model predicts. Weakness (reductionism): It reduces complex consumer responses to three emotional dimensions.
items.markingKey: 2 marks for each point: 1 mark identification, 1 mark explanation in the context of the study [4]

items.stem: A shopping centre in Colombo has falling visitor numbers. The manager, Felix, wants to make it a more pleasant place to spend time. Explain one problem in measuring whether the changes work.
items.answer: Other factors such as season, promotions or the economy also affect visitor numbers, so improvements cannot be attributed only to atmosphere.
items.markingKey: 1 mark confounding factors; 1 mark explained [2]

items.stem: Ines compared average spend per diner (in dollars) on evenings when menu prices included “$” and evenings when they were plain numbers. Table: Average spend per diner ($) — Plain numbers: 34, 35, 37, 33, 35, 28, 31. With currency symbol: 30, 28, 27, 34, 27, 31, 29. Name the experimental design used in this study and explain one weakness of using this design here.
items.answer: Independent measures: different participants take part in each condition. Weakness: participant variables (individual differences between the two groups) may explain the difference in the DV instead of the IV.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct design; 1 mark: weakness explained in context [2]

items.stem: Mateo compared average spend per diner (in dollars) on evenings when menu prices included “$” and evenings when they were plain numbers.
